subject: mathematics
question_text: If a, b, c are three vectors, then prove that (a×b)×c = (c·a)b − (c·b)a.

mark_split.label: Write the vectors in component form

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.38 — LAQ chapter 4 Product of Vectors, answer 25. Printed appearances: AP 15,19. The only PROOF in this chapter — every other answer computes with numbers. The book calls it "Lengthy but Easy", and that is fair: there is no trick, only bookkeeping. ONE PRESENTATION CHANGE, made deliberately: the book writes out all nine component terms of each side in full, across most of a page. Those lines are several times wider than this page body, so each side is expanded to its i-component and the pattern for j and k stated in words. Same mathematics, same marked steps, no line that would be truncated.⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer (its page is set two questions to a page in two columns, which takes the margin those tags would occupy). It follows the shape of the split the same chapter DOES print for answer 23 on book p.37, weighting each cross product against the closing step. The book's chapter header carries ★★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q22 is the Product of Vectors slot. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Expand (c·a)b − (c·b)a.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say what you do to each side and how they meet.

steps.label: Write in components
steps.margin_note: First mark. This is an identity about EVERY triple of vectors, so it cannot use particular numbers. Components with subscripts are what make the proof general.
steps.memory_tip: This is an identity about EVERY triple, so it cannot use particular numbers. Subscripted components make it general.
lines: a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k,  b = b₁i + b₂j + b₃k,

recall.must_convey: That the three vectors are written in general component form with subscripts, because the identity must hold for all vectors.
accept: write a b and c in general component form with subscripts one two three
take general vectors with components rather than numbers
set up a one i plus a two j plus a three k and so on
general components tho rasta, numbers tho kaadu
use subscripted components so the proof is general

steps.why: A numerical example would only check one case. Subscripted components prove it for all of them at once.
common_mistakes: Proving it with particular numbers, which proves nothing in general.
Using the same subscript for two different vectors.

steps.label: Find a×b
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The standard cross-product determinant, but with letters. Write the j term with its sign already absorbed — it makes the next step readable.
steps.memory_tip: The usual determinant, with letters. Absorb the j sign now so the next step reads cleanly.

lines.text: a \times b = \begin{vmatrix} i & j & k \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That a×b is expanded as a determinant in components, giving the three bracketed expressions.
accept: expand the determinant with the components to get the three brackets
a cross b in component form with a two b three minus a three b two and so on
write the cross product determinant with letters
components tho determinant expand cheyyali
the cross product gives three bracketed terms

steps.why: This vector is the left-hand side of the outer cross product, so its components become the first row of the next determinant.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus on the j term rather than absorbing it into the bracket.
Swapping the order of the subscripts inside a bracket.

steps.label: Expand the left side
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Cross that result with c, then multiply out. Only the i component is written in full below — j and k follow exactly the same pattern with the letters rotated.
steps.memory_tip: Write only the i component in full; j and k follow the same pattern with the letters rotated.
lines: Now cross with c. The i component of (a×b)×c is
The j and k components follow the same pattern

recall.must_convey: That (a×b) is crossed with c and multiplied out, and that each component is a four-term expression — the i one being a₃b₁c₃ − a₁b₃c₃ − a₁b₂c₂ + a₂b₁c₂.
accept: cross a cross b with c and expand, each component has four terms
multiply out the second cross product to get four terms per component
the i component works out to four terms and j and k follow the same pattern
rendo cross product expand cheste prathi component ki four terms vasthai
expand the outer cross product in components

steps.why: Four terms per component is what the right-hand side must also produce. Counting them is the quickest check that nothing has been dropped.
common_mistakes: Dropping a term when multiplying out.
Expanding all three components in full and running out of time and space.

steps.label: Expand the right side
steps.margin_note: Three marks. c·a and c·b are NUMBERS, each a sum of three products. Multiplying them into b and a gives six terms per component, of which two always cancel.
steps.memory_tip: c·a and c·b are NUMBERS. Multiplying them in gives six terms per component, two of which always cancel.
lines: The a₁b₁c₁ terms cancel, leaving four terms.   …(2)

recall.must_convey: That c·a and c·b are scalars, and that multiplying them into b and a leaves four terms per component after the a₁b₁c₁ terms cancel.
accept: c dot a and c dot b are numbers, multiply them into b and a and the matching terms cancel leaving four
expand the right hand side, the a one b one c one terms cancel out
six terms per component but two cancel leaving four
c dot a and c dot b scalars, multiply cheste rendu terms cancel avthai
the right side also gives four terms per component
heard_as: a one b one c one

steps.why: The cancellation is the heart of the proof: the term that appears in both products is exactly the one that must vanish for the two sides to match.
common_mistakes: Missing the cancellation and being left with six terms that will not match.

steps.label: Compare and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The four surviving terms on each side are the same four. Say that they match — a proof by expansion is only finished when the comparison is stated.
steps.memory_tip: The four survivors on each side are the same four. Say so — expansion is not a proof until compared.
lines: The four terms in (1) and the four in (2) are
identical, and the same holds for j and k.

recall.must_convey: That the expansions of the two sides give identical terms, so the identity is proved.
accept: the terms on both sides match so the identity is proved
from one and two the two sides are identical
comparing the expansions shows they are equal
rendu sides terms same, so identity proved
both expansions give the same four terms

steps.why: Expanding both sides is not a proof until you say they agree. That last sentence is the step the marks are actually for.
common_mistakes: Expanding both sides and never stating that they match.
Checking the i component only and not saying the others follow.
